dedupe_keys.name: effects of disaster relief insurance on drought impacts in southwest oklahoma review of regional studies 2024

description: This case study quantifies the direct and indirect economic losses from exceptional droughts between 2000 and 2021 in five counties of southwest Oklahoma, and how Federal Crop Insurance Program indemnities for corn, cotton and wheat reduced them. A multi-regional input-output model built with IMPLAN links the hardest-hit region of Harmon, Jackson and Tillman counties, a neighbouring region of Kiowa and Greer counties and the rest of Oklahoma. It was written by Katherine Welch of Louisiana Tech University and Dayton Lambert, Lixia Lambert and Amy Hagerman of Oklahoma State University and published in the Review of Regional Studies, volume 54, in 2024. Coverage is five rural counties whose economies depend on crops and livestock. The article is available free as a PDF, under the Southern Regional Science Association's copyright. Findings: drought cost an average of 163 million dollars of output, 1,084 jobs and 67 million dollars of value added per drought year, and indemnities cut losses by 54 to 63%, helped by a bumper wheat crop and record cattle prices. Caveats: input-output models assume fixed production relationships, and results cover only three insured crops. For simulation it shows how drought losses cascade from farms to other sectors and how insurance payouts dampen them. It is related to the IMPLAN record in this catalogue, the modelling system used.
